children: Former White House AI and crypto czar
David Sacks

said the political debate over artificial intelligence (AI) is shifting from whether to accelerate or slow AI development to whether the technology should remain open and decentralized or become controlled by a few powerful companies.
AI Debate Shifts To Open vs. Closed
On Saturday, in a post on
X
, Sacks shared a clip from the
All-In Podcast
and wrote: "The political debate over AI is shifting from accelerationist vs doomer to decentralized/open vs centralized/closed."

In the podcast discussion, he said the previous AI debate had largely centered on "accelerationists and decels or doomers," but argued that the conversation is now changing as AI adoption continues to grow.
"I kind of just see myself as a realist," Sacks said. "I think that the technology is going to happen. Someone’s going to develop it. And I’d rather it be the United States as opposed to China."
Sacks argued that AI will be difficult to stop because consumers and businesses are driving demand for the technology.
"The adoption is pulling this whole thing forward," he said.

He said the next political fight will focus on whether AI develops into "an open market where there’s lots of decentralized models" with "checks and balances" or "a highly centralized solution" dominated by a few frontier companies.
Centralized AI Raises Civil Liberties Concerns
Jason Calacanis
warned about the risks of closed systems, telling Sacks, "They’re closed models. And they can rug pull you, Sacks, at any time."
Sacks also argued that leading AI companies could seek greater regulatory oversight while influencing how those rules are written.
Sacks pointed to
Anthropic
CEO
Dario Amodei

‘s concerns about sufficiently advanced open models, arguing that Amodei’s position could lead toward greater centralized control. Amodei, however, has said Anthropic does not support a ban on open-weight models and has instead called for targeted measures including safety testing for sufficiently capable models.
Sacks said the issue could ultimately cross party lines, arguing that "most conservatives, most libertarians are going to see the threat to civil liberties" and favor open AI.
The political debate over AI is shifting from accelerationist vs doomer to decentralized/open vs centralized/closed.
